# Introduction

This report generates the results reported in our paper (but not the figures---see the script `final_paper_figures.R` for those).


```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 5,
                      fig.height = 3,
                      out.width = "75%",
                      message = FALSE,
                      fig.align = "center")
options(list(dplyr.summarise.inform = FALSE))
theme_set( theme_classic() )

source( here::here( "empirical/load_and_prep_empirical_results.R" ) )



```

# Some statistics on the studies

Our count of studies is the following:
```{r}
whole_studies <- studies %>%
  group_by( Project,Collection, blocked ) %>%
  summarise( n = n() )
table( whole_studies$Collection, whole_studies$blocked ) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

Our count of outcomes is the following:

```{r}
table( studies$Collection, studies$blocked ) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```


Some statistics about the studies across the `r nrow(filter( studies, blocked=="Blocked"))` outcomes:
```{r}
studies %>%
  filter( blocked == "Blocked" ) %>%
  pivot_longer( c( n, ncv, nbar, J, Jcv, K, cluster_ICC, block_ICC, R2.1, R2.2, p.tx, R_ate, R_se ),
                names_to="statistic", values_to="value" ) %>%
  group_by( statistic ) %>%
  summarise( mean = mean(value),
             median = median( value ),
             sd = sd(value),
             min = min( value ),
             Q10 = quantile(value, 0.1),
             Q90 = quantile(value, 0.9),
             max = max( value ) ) %>%
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)

```


**The 10th and 90th percentile number of individuals, clusters and blocks are around: 850 to 17,500 (individuals), 30 to 495 (clusters), and 5 to 85 (blocks).**

```{r}
blocked = filter( studies, blocked =="Blocked" )

n = quantile( blocked$n, c(0.1, 0.9) )
J = quantile( blocked$J, c(0.1, 0.9) )
K = quantile( blocked$K, c(0.1, 0.9) )
bind_rows( n=n, J=J, K=K, .id = "unit" ) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

**Cut-off for "low" degrees of freedom**

Low is strictly less than 10

# Some statistics on our estimators

The number of large ranges of SE (2x or more) and ATE (0.10 or more) is the following (*** means yes, blank means no):

```{r}
table( `big ATE range` = studies$big_ate, `big SE ratio` = studies$big_se ) 
```


## The number of ATE ranges greater than 0.10 and 0.05

```{r}
ranges %>%
  group_by( group, measure ) %>%
  filter( str_detect( measure, "ate") ) %>%
  summarise( n = n(),
             n_10 = sum( Range >= 0.10 ),
             big_10 = n_10 / n,
             n_05 = sum( Range >= 0.05 ),
             big_5 = n_05 / n ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )

```

## How often Standard errors are large

```{r}
ranges %>%
  group_by( group, measure ) %>%
  filter( !str_detect( measure, "ate") ) %>%
  summarise( n = n(),
              n_1.2 = sum( Range >= 1.2 ),
             big_1.2 = n_1.2 / n,
            n_1.5 = sum( Range >= 1.5 ),
             big_1.5 = n_1.5 / n,
             n_2 = sum( Range >= 2 ),
             big_2 = n_2 / n,
             max = max( Range ) ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )

```

## Stability connected to df

**When DF are low, the ratio of the largest to smallest standard error is always greater than 1.5x. When DF are high, only 6 out of 34 outcomes have a ratio above 1.5.**

Note: The above claim is no longer true, now that we have fixed the Fully Interacted issue.

```{r}
ranges %>%
  group_by( low_df, group, measure ) %>%
  filter( !str_detect( measure, "ate") ) %>%
  summarise( n = n(),
             n_1.2 = sum( Range >= 1.2 ),
             big_1.2 = n_1.2 / n,
             n_1.5 = sum( Range >= 1.5 ),
             big_1.5 = n_1.5 / n,
             n_2 = sum( Range >= 2 ),
             big_2 = n_2 / n ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )

```


## Fully interacted estimator notes (now defunct)

**To consider how much trouble the fully interacted models are causing, we exclude them and recalculate the ratios (see Figure 5). Doing so dramatically changes the story. For example, the largest estimated standard error is 1.5x the smallest estimated standard error in only 10 percent of cases without the fully-interacted models, down from 48 percent when considering all estimators. The ratio never exceeds 1.7 once the fully-interacted models are excluded.**

See above tables.

**Even in Figure 3 we see estimated standard errors that are 20 percent different across estimators in over 20 percent of the cases we examined.**

See above tables


## When are SE estimators defined?

**While this model-free approach is appealing in theory, in practice this means design-based standard errors can only be estimated if every block X experimental arm has at least two or more clusters. Only three studies in our sample meet this condition; consequently, the design-based standard errors do not exist for XX out of 50 outcomes when the fully-interacted model (for individual or aggregate data) is implemented. The same limitation applies to heteroskedastic robust standard errors. For most outcomes, there are only 13 estimated standard errors, rather than 19 (See Supplemental Excel Spreadsheet 1).**

This table counts the number of undefined estimators within each group given the set of covariates included.

```{r}
#cc <- combined %>%
#  dplyr::select( UniqueID, Covariates, Estimator, ATE_hat_std, SE_hat_std )
#skimr::skim( cc )
combined %>%
  group_by( Covariates, Estimator ) %>%
  summarise( n = n(),
             n_ATE = sum( is.na( ATE_hat_std ) ),
             n_SE = sum( is.na( SE_hat_std ) ) ) %>%
  pivot_wider( names_from=Covariates, values_from=c(n_ATE, n_SE) ) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

This table counts the number of estimates for each outcome that are undefined (the different columns correspond to adjusting for all covariates, a single best covariate, or no covariates):

```{r}
combined %>%
  group_by( UniqueID, Covariates ) %>%
  summarise( n = n(),
             n_ATE = sum( is.na( ATE_hat_std ) ),
             n_SE = sum( is.na( SE_hat_std ) ) ) %>%
  pivot_wider( names_from=Covariates, values_from=c(n_ATE, n_SE) ) %>%
  knitr::kable()
```

# ATE Ranges

## Studies with a high range (more than 0.15) of ATE estimates

```{r}
ss <- studies %>%
  filter( blocked == "Blocked", R_ate > 0.15 ) %>%
  dplyr::select( Project, UniqueID, K, J, n, cons_df, R_ate, R_ate_Clu, R_ate_Per )

ss %>%

```


### High range within Estimand

Still a threshold of 0.15.

```{r}
ss <- studies %>%
  filter( blocked == "Blocked", R_ate > 0.15 | R_ate_Clu > 0.10 | R_ate_Per > 0.10 ) %>%
  dplyr::select( Project, UniqueID, K, J, n, cons_df, R_ate, R_ate_Clu, R_ate_Per )

ss %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )

cc <- combined %>%
  dplyr::filter( UniqueID %in% ss$UniqueID, Covariates == "best" ) 

cc %>%
  group_by( UniqueID, num_singletons, ncv, Jcv ) %>% 
  summarise( ATE_min = min( ATE_hat_std, na.rm=TRUE ),
             ATE_max = max( ATE_hat_std, na.rm=TRUE ),
             range = ATE_max - ATE_min,
             SE_avg = mean( SE_hat_std, na.rm=TRUE ),
             n_est = n(),
             n_def = sum( !is.na( ATE_hat_std ) ) ) %>%
  arrange( UniqueID ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )
```


```{r, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 6, out.height= "70%" }

ggplot( cc, aes(Estimator, ATE_hat_std, color = Estimand ) ) +
  facet_wrap( ~ UniqueID, scales="free_x", nrow=1 ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_point( data=filter(cc,str_detect( Estimator, "MLM" ) ), 
              color="black", shape = 21, size = 3 ) +
  coord_flip()
```




```{r}
rr <- rangesW %>%
  filter( Covariates =="best", group=="estimand" ) %>%
  mutate( cons_df_adj = ifelse( cons_df > 30, 30, cons_df ) ) 

rr %>%
ggplot( aes(cons_df_adj, Range ) ) +
  facet_wrap( has_single ~ Estimand,  nrow=1 ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method="lm", se=FALSE)


rr %>%
ggplot( aes(cons_df_adj, Range ) ) +
  facet_wrap( . ~ Estimand,  nrow=1 ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(se=FALSE)
```

Range does go up as expected with average SE increasing:
```{r}
rr %>%
ggplot( aes(SE_avg, Range ) ) +
  facet_wrap( has_single ~ Estimand,  nrow=1 ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method="lm", se=FALSE)

```


We can see if range depends on variation in block or cluster size:
```{r}
rr2 <- rangesW %>%
  filter( Covariates =="best", group=="all" ) %>%
  mutate( cons_df_adj = ifelse( cons_df > 30, 30, cons_df ) ) 

ggplot( rr2, aes(Jcv, Range ) ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method="lm", se=FALSE)

ggplot( rr2, aes(ncv, Range ) ) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(se=FALSE)
```


We can use trees to predict what predicts larger range:

```{r}
source( here::here( "analysis/Simulation_Write_Up/create_analysis_tree.R" ) )
tree1<-create_analysis_tree(rr2,
                            "Range",
                            predictor_vars = c( "cons_df", "ncv", "Jcv", "SE_avg", "R2.1", "R2.2", "has_single", "cluster_ICC", "block_ICC" ) )
```

If we drop the average SE we get this:
```{r}
tree1<-create_analysis_tree(rr2,
                            "Range",
                            predictor_vars = c( "cons_df", "ncv", "Jcv", "R2.1", "R2.2",
                                                "has_single", "cluster_ICC", "block_ICC" ) )
```

These trees shows that uncertainty drives larger differences, and also that greater variation in cluster size drives larger differences, especially if there is variation in the cluster means.

If we look within estimand, we see that our datasets with larger R2.1 and no singletons are larger ranges (assuming the SEs are generally large):

```{r}
tree2<-create_analysis_tree(rr,
                            "Range",
                            predictor_vars = c( "cons_df", "Estimand", "ncv", "Jcv", "SE_avg", "R2.1", "R2.2", "has_single", "cluster_ICC", "block_ICC" ) )

```

## Comparing low DF to high DF studies

```{r}
ra <- rr2 %>%

ra$ratio = ra$avg_rng / min( ra$avg_rng )
```

# Standard Errors


## Studies with a high ratio of SE estimates


Here are all the studies with an SE range above 1.75.

```{r}
CUT = 1.75
ss <- studies %>%
  filter( blocked == "Blocked", R_se > CUT | R_se_Clu > CUT | R_se_Per > CUT ) %>%
  dplyr::select( Project, UniqueID, K, J, n, cons_df, R_se, R_se_Clu, R_se_Per )

ss %>%
  arrange( UniqueID ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )

combined %>%
  dplyr::filter( UniqueID %in% ss$UniqueID, Covariates == "best" ) %>%
  group_by( UniqueID, cons_df, num_singletons ) %>% 
  summarise( SE_min = min( SE_hat_std, na.rm=TRUE ),
             SE_max = max( SE_hat_std, na.rm=TRUE ),
             n_est = n(),
             n_def = sum( !is.na( SE_hat_std ) ) ) %>%
  arrange( UniqueID ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 4 )
```

The SEs for the troublesome studies:

```{r}
  stud <- combined |>
    filter(UniqueID %in% ss$UniqueID, !is.na(SE_hat_std), Covariates =="best" ) |>
    mutate(
      Estimator = factor(Estimator),
      Estimator = fct_reorder(Estimator, SE_hat_std, .na_rm = TRUE)
    )
  
  ggplot(stud, aes(Estimator, SE_hat_std, pch=Estimand, col = Covariates)) +
    facet_wrap( ~ UniqueID, scales="free" ) +
    geom_point() +
    geom_hline( yintercept = 0 ) +
    coord_flip() +
    labs(
      title = "SE estimates",
      subtitle = "(For defined estimators)"
    )

```

## How much do SE ratios go down within Estimand?

In the following we look at how much the SE ratios shrink going within estimand.

```{r include=FALSE}
 # Looking at how range decreases as we go within estimand
source( here::here( "empirical/calculate_all_ranges.R" ) )
  ss <- summary_stats_estimand %>%
    filter(Covariates == "best") %>%
    dplyr::select( UniqueID, Estimand, Ratio ) 
  ss
  ss1 <- summary_stats %>%
    filter(Covariates == "best") %>%
    dplyr::select(UniqueID, Range, Ratio)
  ssf <- left_join(ss, ss1, by = 'UniqueID')
  
  knitr::kable( ssf, digits = 2 )
  ggplot( ssf, aes( Ratio.y, Ratio.x ) ) +
    facet_wrap( ~ Estimand ) +
    geom_point() +
    coord_fixed() +
    geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, lty = 2, col = 'red') +
    labs( x = "Overall ratio", y = "Within Estimand Ratio" )
  
  ssf %>% 
    mutate( rat = Ratio.x / Ratio.y ) %>%
    group_by( Estimand ) %>%
    summarise( mean_rat = mean( rat ),
               sd_rat = sd( rat ) ) %>%
    knitr::kable( digits=2 )
```


# Are SEs for cluster weight smaller than individual?

```{r}
library( lme4 )

combined$Covariates = factor( combined$Covariates,
                              levels = c( "best", "none", "all" ) )
M = lmer( log( SE_hat_std ) ~ Estimand + Covariates + has_single + (1|Estimator) + (1|UniqueID) + (1|Estimand:UniqueID),
          data=combined )
arm::display(M)
exp( fixef( M ) ) 
```


## Which estimators tend to be most extreme?

```{r}
extreme <- combined %>%
  filter( Covariates == "best", !is.na( SE_hat_std ) ) %>%
  group_by( UniqueID ) %>%
  mutate( ratio = max( SE_hat_std ) / min(SE_hat_std ),
          extreme = rank( SE_hat_std, ties.method = "first" ) <= 2 |
          rank( SE_hat_std, ties.method = "first" ) >= n() - 1 ) %>%
  filter( ratio > 1.25 ) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by( Estimator, Estimand ) %>%
  summarise( n_def = n(),
             n_extreme = sum( extreme ),
             per = n_extreme / n_def )

extreme %>%
  arrange( per ) %>%
  knitr::kable( digits = 2 )


```
